extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students of literature/philosophy interested in Montaigne
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Montaigne's essay passages about animals and what they reveal about human judgment, reason, and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value ordinary observation as much as the unusual
rubrics_metrics.description: We more admire and value things that are unusual and strange than those of ordinary observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against privileging exotic or dramatic examples over everyday ones; he insists that careful attention to animals we commonly see will reveal wonders equal to remote or ancient anecdotes. Example: the essayist says he has 'insisted upon these examples' but that ordinary local animals could provide equally wonderful effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid condemning unfamiliar differences as stupidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Who did not attribute it to stupidity and want of common sense to see them mute, ignorant of the French tongue, ignorant of our salutations and cringes... All that seems strange to us, and that we do not understand, we condemn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that behavioral or cultural difference implies lack of intelligence or worth. Montaigne uses travelers and foreign peoples (and by analogy animals) to show that unfamiliarity breeds unjust negative judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer by comparison but acknowledge limits of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: They have several conditions like to ours; from those we may, by comparison, draw some conjecture: but by those qualities that are particular to themselves, what know we what to make of them!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarities between humans and animals to form hypotheses, but be modest about conclusions regarding traits concealed from our observation. Montaigne recommends cautious, comparative reasoning rather than overconfident generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize animal problem-solving and tool use as signs of subtle capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Plutarch: a dog on board a ship fetched stones and let them fall into a jar till he made the oil rise so high that he could reach it; ravens do the same; elephants raise stones and logs to rescue trapped comrades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat demonstrations of foresight, manipulation of environment, and tool-like behavior as legitimate evidence of intelligence rather than mere instinct. Examples include the stone-in-jar dog, ravens, and cooperative elephant rescue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge nonverbal communication and social interchange among animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleanthes’ observation of ants carrying the dead and performing mutual exchanges was taken as evidence that creatures 'that have no voice are not, nevertheless, without intercourse and mutual communication'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret complex group behaviors (rituals, transfer, cooperative journeys) as forms of communication and social organization; Montaigne cites ants, bees, and fishes as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer absence of inner life or 'religion' from lack of human-like signs
rubrics_metrics.description: The elephants ... are observed to lift up their trunk like arms, and, fixing their eyes towards the rising of the sun, continue long in meditation and contemplation... But because we do not see any such signs in other animals, we cannot for that conclude that they are without religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concluding that animals lack reflective or ritualized behavior simply because they do not display human analogues; Montaigne cautions about drawing negative inferences from our limited observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat adaptive, anticipatory behavior as cognitive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen of Cyzicus observed the hedge-hog's burrow openings and predicted winds; the ants air and dry their seed, nibble grain to prevent germination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of anticipating environmental change or managing resources should be read as prudence and foresight. Montaigne uses hedgehog and ant examples to argue animals possess practical intelligence relevant to survival and planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish passive from active biological change when inferring agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The caméléon takes her colour from the place upon which she is laid; but the polypus gives himself what colour he pleases, according to occasion, either to conceal himself from what he fears, or from what he has a design to seize: in the caméléon 'tis a passive, but in the polypus 'tis an active, change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observing phenomena like color change, determine whether it is reactive (passive) or intentional (active) before attributing agency or deliberate design to the animal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge animals' moral-like affections (fidelity, gratitude, friendship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances: dogs keeping watch over dead masters and avenging them; Hyrcanus the dog of Lysimachus starving and leaping into the funeral pyre; the lion that remembered Androdus who healed its wounded foot and later protected him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat demonstrations of attachment, loyalty, and reciprocal behaviour as morally significant emotions rather than mere reflex; Montaigne uses numerous anecdotes (dogs, lions, elephants) to show animals capable of such affections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe social cooperation and mutual assistance as organizing principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: whale followed by a guide-fish; the wren acting as sentinel for the crocodile; naker and shrimp cooperating to trap prey; mullets and other fishes cutting lines to free companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize symbiosis, sentinel behavior, and coordinated group maneuvers as evidence of complex social arrangements and role differentiation among animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of human vanity about war and greatness; large human actions rest on petty causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne likens armies to disturbed ant-hills and argues the same passions move a gnat and an elephant; 'This furious monster... is yet man--feeble, calamitous, and miserable man!' Small causes (a stumble, a dream, a croaking of ravens) can overthrow great forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read martial spectacle with irony: spectacular scale does not imply superior cause or nobler motive. Montaigne uses this as a criterion to judge the true nature and fragility of human grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast human artificial desires with animals' natural moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Desires are classified: natural and necessary (eat, drink), natural but not necessary (coupling), and neither natural nor necessary (most human desires). 'Animals are much more regular than we, and keep themselves with greater moderation within the limits nature has prescribed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use animals as a mirror to critique human extravagance and artificial appetites; Montaigne suggests animals often better observe natural limits and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete anecdotes as evidence but remain aware of anecdotal limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay compiles many singular stories (elephants separating barley, dogs leading thieves to justice, halcyon calming the sea while nesting) as evidence for claims about animal faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Montaigne relies on illustrative anecdotes to make broader philosophical points, one should note the evidentiary limitations of isolated stories and balance them with broader observation and skepticism.
